A forecast report should include confidence intervals, calibration diagnostics, and explicit uncertainty. If the model cannot cite the data and computation behind a number, the number should not enter the investment process.
why: Fluency around a number feels like evidence for it, but small numerical errors drive large position changes. The fix is architectural — audited code computes, the model explains — not a better prompt.
uw: Use when an LLM-generated forecast, ratio, or expected return is about to enter a report, model, or trade.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Collusion without a conversation
steal: Agents optimized independently can learn strategies that soften competition or align behavior through the environment. In finance, analogous mechanisms could appear in pricing, liquidity provision, collateral terms, or execution. Monitoring must therefore examine outcome patterns and incentives, not only source-code similarity or explicit messages.
why: Coordination needs neither communication nor shared code — independent learners can discover mutually accommodating behavior through the market itself. That makes code audits and chat-log reviews structurally blind to the risk; only outcome patterns reveal it.
uw: Use when assessing competition or systemic risk from multiple independently deployed trading or pricing agents.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Governance makes good uses repeatable
steal: The central purpose of governance is not to prevent the use of LLMs. It is to make valuable uses repeatable while keeping failure within tolerable bounds.
why: This reframes governance from veto to engineering discipline: repeatability of the wins, boundedness of the losses. It is the definition you hand to a business line that reads every control proposal as innovation-blocking.
uw: Use when a governance or model-risk proposal is being dismissed as bureaucracy that slows the business down.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Freeze everything at the forecast origin
steal: A valid evaluation must freeze not only the price history but also the prompt, retrieval store, tools, memory, model version, and researcher workflow at each forecast origin.
why: Backtests leak through channels most quants never freeze: the prompt, the retrieval index, the agent's memory, even the researcher's own iteration over prompt variants. Freezing prices alone leaves the impressive-but-invalid result intact.
uw: Use when reviewing or designing a backtest of an LLM-based forecasting or trading system.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: The pipeline, not the point solution
steal: Large Language Models in finance are best understood as part of a pipeline rather than as a point solution. Raw documents, time series, and market feeds are curated, normalized, and embedded; retrieval layers keep knowledge current; generation is constrained by financial identities, accounting rules, and risk limits; policies are aligned and evaluated; and decisions are executed within a framework of governance and oversight.
why: Upgrading the model is the least interesting move in the stack: if retrieval is stale, numbers are uncited, and decisions are ungated, a better generator just produces better-looking failures faster. Budget and scrutiny should flow to the pipeline joints, not the model checkpoint.
uw: When a team frames an LLM project as 'pick the best model,' reframe the plan around the pipeline: curation, retrieval, constraint, alignment, governance.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Four layers have to agree
steal: The architecture has four layers, illustrated in Figure 11.1 . Evidence and assurance flow upward from infrastructure and behavior to risk and accountability, while policy, limits, permissions, and escalation rules flow downward. The layers are interdependent rather than sequential maturity levels.
why: Controls fail at layer boundaries, not inside layers: a calibrated model fed stale data, or fresh data flowing through unpermissioned tools, breaks the system even though each layer 'works.' The four layers are the checklist for where to look when something goes wrong.
uw: When designing or auditing a financial LLM system, verify all four layers agree — infrastructure, behavior, risk, accountability — instead of certifying the model alone.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: A fine-tuning run is defined by its contract
steal: a financial fine-tuning experiment is not defined by a model name and a training set. It is defined by a decision date, a permissible information set, a task loss, a calibration protocol, and an approval boundary.
why: Model name plus training set is how demos are described; decision date plus information set plus loss plus calibration plus approval boundary is how production systems are defended. Without the contract, a fine-tune can't be reproduced, audited, or blamed — it can only be admired.
uw: Before greenlighting any fine-tuning run, demand the contract: what data as of when, what loss, what calibration check, who approved it.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: RAG's two controls
steal: Two things distinguish it from a generic one, and both are controls rather than models. The availability filter D ≤ t admits only documents that existed at the decision time t , which is what stops a backtest from reading tomorrow’s filing. The claim-level verifier checks each material claim A i against its retrieved evidence bundle E i before the answer is released, which is what stops a fluent answer from being an unsupported one.
why: A RAG system fails in exactly two places that matter: letting the future leak in (the availability filter) and letting fluent prose out without evidence (the claim verifier). Everything else — embeddings, chunking, reranking — is optimization inside those two guardrails.
uw: When evaluating a RAG build, check the two controls first: does retrieval enforce the decision-time cutoff, and does anything verify claims against evidence before release?
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: MCP is a protocol, not a governance framework
steal: MCP is an interoperability protocol, not a complete governance framework. A regulated institution must therefore place a separate financial control envelope around MCP-based tool use. This envelope includes identity, least-privilege authorization, typed tool contracts, point-in-time evidence checks, deterministic numerical recomputation, approval gates, idempotent execution, and tamper-evident audit records.
why: A protocol standardizes how tools talk; it says nothing about who may call them, with what authority, or what happens when they lie. Treating MCP as governance is like treating TCP as a firewall — the envelope has to be built separately, or every connected tool inherits the model's authority by default.
uw: When wiring MCP tools into a regulated workflow, build the control envelope first: identity, least-privilege auth, typed contracts, approval gates, audit records.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Every artifact carries its provenance
steal: a sentence that reaches the memo without one is not a stylistic lapse but a broken audit trail.
why: The chain breaks at table extraction — where a structured number gets flattened into prose and loses its row, column, and timestamp. Once that happens the memo looks rigorous and is unauditable; the fix is provenance at the artifact level, not prettier writing.
uw: When a generated memo contains numbers, trace each one back to its source artifact before trusting it — a number without lineage is decoration.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: One scalar reward can't hold compliance
steal: Capturing all of these dimensions in a single scalar reward is challenging; in practice, institutions often train separate reward models for different preference dimensions and combine their signals.
why: A single scalar forces rigor, calibration, tone, compliance, and readability to trade off against each other inside one number — so the model learns whichever dimension is easiest to game. Separate reward models per dimension keep the trade-offs visible and auditable.
uw: When reviewing an RLHF setup for a compliance-sensitive task, ask how many reward dimensions are trained separately — one scalar for everything is a red flag.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Performance is not a single-number property
steal: For generative systems, quality is vector-valued. A financial LLM is not judged only by a semantic metric such as ROUGE, BLEU, cosine similarity, or pairwise preference. It is judged by a tuple: (3) covering task usefulness, evidence faithfulness, numerical consistency, calibration, policy compliance, latency, and cost.
why: A model that tops the semantic-similarity leaderboard can still hallucinate numbers, leak the future, and cost a fortune to run. Judging by one metric optimizes for the metric; judging by the tuple forces the trade-offs into the open.
uw: When comparing models or vendors, demand the full tuple — usefulness, faithfulness, numerical consistency, calibration, compliance, latency, cost — not a single score.
author: Miquel Noguer i Alonso

title: Bridging the Gap: Enhancing SNA Within the Marine Corps Intelligence Community
steal: Social network analysis (SNA) is a worthwhile intelligence method that the Marine Corps intelligence enterprise (MCISRE) does not currently use — survey and interview findings show Marine Corps intelligence personnel are not proficient in SNA and routinely confuse it with link analysis and social media analysis (SMA), with causal factors mapped across the DOTmLPF pillars.
why: It documents a capability gap by name — the analytic method the force's own roadmaps call for is the one its people can't distinguish from two adjacent techniques.
uw: A tool nobody can tell apart from its neighbors is a tool nobody can use — naming the confusion precisely (SNA vs. link analysis vs. social media analysis) is the first step to closing the gap.
book: Bridging the Gap: Enhancing SNA Within the Marine Corps Intelligence Community
author: Robert C. Schotter

title: Optical Theory Improvements to Space Domain Awareness
steal: The dissertation introduces two models for universal superadiabatic quantum computing built on counter-diabatic Hamiltonians — one using superadiabatic quantum teleportation as a primitive for arbitrary n-qubit gates, the other using controlled superadiabatic evolutions to implement n-controlled gates with simple time-independent Hamiltonians — and argues via the quantum speed limit that superadiabatic evolution is in principle compatible with arbitrarily small time intervals, constrained by energetic cost.
why: It's a concrete attack on adiabatic quantum computing's main weakness — slowness — showing the speed limit is about energy budget, not an intrinsic time floor.
uw: When a theorem limits your speed, check what the limit actually prices — here the "speed limit" prices energy, so the engineering question becomes how much energy you can afford, not how fast physics allows.
book: Optical Theory Improvements to Space Domain Awareness
author: Tyler J. Hardy

title: The Federal Task Force on Housing and Urban Development and the Limits of Participatory Democracy, 1968-1969
steal: The 1969 Hellyer Task Force on Housing and Urban Development — launched during Trudeaumania's participatory-politics wave after a Canada-wide public consultation — blended "liberal" and "deliberative" types of participatory democracy in a four-part typology the thesis proposes; the differing political approaches of Paul Hellyer and Pierre Elliott Trudeau help explain the Cabinet's hostile reception of the report and Hellyer's resignation in April 1969.
why: Public consultation doesn't fail in one way — the thesis gives a taxonomy (liberal, deliberative, radical, revolutionary) for diagnosing exactly which kind of participation a reform actually invited.
uw: When a consultation exercise collapses, ask which democracy it was practicing — Hellyer's task force asked for input in one register and was judged in another.
book: The Federal Task Force on Housing and Urban Development and the Limits of Participatory Democracy, 1968-1969
author: Brendan Nicholas Gemmell

title: Atalhos para Adiabaticidade e Aplicacoes em Computacao Quantica (Shortcuts to Adiabaticity and Applications in Quantum Computation)
steal: The dissertation introduces two models for universal superadiabatic quantum computing built on counter-diabatic Hamiltonians — one using superadiabatic quantum teleportation as a primitive for arbitrary n-qubit gates, the other using controlled superadiabatic evolutions to implement n-controlled gates with simple time-independent Hamiltonians — and argues via the quantum speed limit that superadiabatic evolution is in principle compatible with arbitrarily small time intervals, constrained by energetic cost.
why: It's a concrete attack on adiabatic quantum computing's main weakness — slowness — showing the speed limit is about energy budget, not an intrinsic time floor.
uw: When a theorem limits your speed, check what the limit actually prices — here the "speed limit" prices energy, so the engineering question becomes how much energy you can afford, not how fast physics allows.
book: Atalhos para Adiabaticidade e Aplicacoes em Computacao Quantica (Shortcuts to Adiabaticity and Applications in Quantum Computation)
author: Alan Costa dos Santos

title: Using Mathematical Modeling and Set-Based Design Principles to Recommend an Existing CVL Design
steal: Nimitz- and Ford-class supercarriers' size and expense are a strategic vulnerability in a future maritime conflict; light aircraft carriers (CVLs) would reduce the risk to grand strategy and cut life-cycle and operating costs, provided a CVL can carry the needed mix of rotary-wing, fixed-wing, electronic-attack, and unmanned aircraft — and set-based design can produce the feasible CVL by mapping the trade space in tonnage, launch method, propulsion, and performance.
why: It puts a method behind the distributed-vs.-concentrated naval debate — instead of point-optimizing one ship, map the whole design space and keep options open until the constraints are known.
uw: When the stakes are high and the future is uncertain, map the trade space before picking the answer — set-based design narrows many options in parallel instead of betting on one.
book: Using Mathematical Modeling and Set-Based Design Principles to Recommend an Existing CVL Design
author: William H. Ehlies

title: Technological Evolution of High Temperature Superconductors
steal: High-temperature superconducting (HTS) cable is nearing full-scale integration — already demonstrated in the commercial electric grid and successfully tested by the Navy (a working HTS degaussing system on a modern U.S. destroyer in 2008), with electric-ship propulsion and high-energy weapons like rail guns and lasers as the next targets; patent-trend analysis projects continued innovation.
why: Superconductors sit at the junction of the energy and naval lanes — a cable that moves power with near-zero loss rewrites both grid economics and warship design.
uw: Patent filings are a leading indicator — when you want to know where a technology is going, count what's being claimed, not what's being announced.
book: Technological Evolution of High Temperature Superconductors
author: Jordan R. White

title: Supply Chain: Wake Up; It is Critical to Military Success
steal: The DOD's global supply chain has no single owner — TRANSCOM and the Defense Logistics Agency form the foundation of the execution mechanism but neither owns the entire process, and the governing legislation, directives, and instructions are ambiguous enough to breed inefficiency. The fix: clear, well-defined roles and responsibilities, a single designated process owner, and one integrated IT system under that owner.
why: "The line between disorder and order lies in logistics" — the thesis documents that the world's most expensive logistics enterprise is governed by ambiguity and personalities, not ownership.
uw: If no one owns the whole process, no one can fix it — ambiguous governance doesn't produce flexibility, it produces drift.
book: Supply Chain: Wake Up; It is Critical to Military Success
author: Christopher E. Dexter

title: Ethics, Eugenics, and Public Education in Georgia (1910-1965)
steal: Georgia's forced sterilization of over 4,000 people from 1939 to 1965 rested on eugenic ideology serving as an "objective" scientific justification for white supremacy and racial hierarchy — and the state's public schools were an active transmission belt, teaching eugenics to the populace.
why: A case study in how a scientific consensus captures institutions — policy, courts, and classrooms moved together on the same "objective" premise.
uw: When science becomes the alibi for state power, follow the teaching — the classroom is where a contested idea becomes the next generation's common sense.
book: Ethics, Eugenics, and Public Education in Georgia (1910-1965)
author: Aaron Gerald Guest Sr.

title: The Triangle Offense: Using Social Movement Theory to Analyze Russia's Gray Zone Strategy
steal: Social Movement Theory's tripartite structure — ideological framing, resource mobilization, political opportunity — gives senior strategists a working model for analyzing gray-zone adversaries: applied to Russia and Ukraine, it identifies the adversary's existing sources of tension, likely vulnerabilities in a target region, and viable countermeasures.
why: The gray zone is named in the thesis as one of the greatest challenges facing the United States; this gives analysts a compact, systematic lens for spotting where an adversary draws strength and where a target region is soft, before the shooting starts.
uw: To counter an adversary's gray-zone playbook, borrow a model from another field — social-movement analysis makes murky influence campaigns legible as framing, funding, and opportunity.
book: The Triangle Offense: Using Social Movement Theory to Analyze Russia's Gray Zone Strategy
author: Alexander V. Simmons

title: Server-based and server-less BYOD solutions to support electronic learning
steal: The Navy can securely deliver eLearning content to service members' personal devices through either a server-based or a server-less BYOD method — both demonstrated with working proofs of concept — creating a low-risk environment that preserves government network security while professional military education keeps moving.
why: At the time, no viable in-policy solution existed anywhere in the Department of the Navy for eLearning on personal devices; the thesis supplied the baseline for secure mobile learning at scale.
uw: When security policy blocks the obvious tool, prototype two paths in parallel — one conventional, one server-less — and let feasibility testing pick the winner.
book: Server-based and server-less BYOD solutions to support electronic learning
author: Joshua C. Benson & Brian R. McCarthy

title: Measuring Resilience
steal: Physiological metrics from commercial wearables can be associated with self-reported assessments to proactively assess resilience and identify service members at risk of compromised resilience — with the OURA ring's PPG sensor, HRV metrics, and sleep algorithms performing well enough to track large cohorts over time.
why: After two decades of war, the military still lacked any tangible way to assess or train resilience; this moves the question from self-report vibes to trackable biometrics.
uw: If you cannot measure the outcome, instrument the proxy — physiological signals can stand in for psychological states once validated against self-reports.
author: Joshua L. Boyle

title: Investigating the effect of Copper (CuI) depletion on the serotonergic neurons and serotonin signalling in the nematode based model
steal: Depleting copper (CuI) with tetrathiomolybdate in C. elegans selectively destroys serotonergic HSN neurons — broken axonal extensions, degraded egg-laying from impaired serotonin release to the vulval muscles — while pharyngeal ADF/NSM neurons stay structurally and functionally intact.
why: It demonstrates differential susceptibility in a clean model — the same trace-element deficiency destroys one neuron population and leaves another untouched, mirroring how Menkes disease patients show selective neurodegeneration.
uw: Vulnerability is cell-type specific — a toxin's damage map tells you more about the system's architecture than about the toxin itself.
book: Investigating the effect of Copper (CuI) depletion on the serotonergic neurons and serotonin signalling in the nematode based model
author: Iram Khan

title: Indo-Slavic lexical isoglosses and the prehistoric dispersal of Indo-Iranian
steal: Shared lexical innovations between Indo-Iranian and Balto-Slavic reveal a period of shared development — the Indo-Slavic linkage — meaning Indo-Iranian did not spread straight eastward from the Core Indo-European homeland; it moved into northeast Europe during the 3rd millennium BCE and only then spread east toward the Urals.
why: It redraws the migration map — a detour through northeast Europe instead of the long-assumed direct eastward push out of the steppe.
uw: Shared vocabulary is a migration map — the words two language branches innovated together trace where their speakers once stood.
book: Indo-Slavic lexical isoglosses and the prehistoric dispersal of Indo-Iranian
author: A.I. Palmér

title: The paradoxical pope: the contemplative and active lives of Gregory the Great
steal: Gregory the Great's monastic years at St. Andrews — the contemplative life — were the preparation that let him steer the Roman Church through plague, famine, and invasion; he reconciled contemplation with action into a model of ecclesiastical leadership, crystallized in the mission of monks to England that secured Rome's central authority into the Middle Ages.
why: Leadership under civilizational collapse — Gregory held the Roman Church together while the empire around it came apart, and the thesis argues his preparation was withdrawal, not war-gaming.
uw: The leader who can hold a crisis is often the one who trained in stillness — contemplative formation can be preparation for action, not retreat from it.
book: The paradoxical pope: the contemplative and active lives of Gregory the Great
author: Elizabeth E. Marvel

title: Seizing the Digital High Ground: Military Operations and Politics in the Social Media Era
steal: Unless the military vastly improves its understanding of social media's utility and invests more in applying it, it risks losing relevance and becoming a blunt instrument for executing political aims and providing security in the 21st century; the British military's current doctrinal view is limited, best characterised as caution, with opinion divided on relative threats and opportunities.
why: It names the mechanism of modern information warfare: social media has decisively altered the speed, scrutiny, and sensitivity of the military's operational environment — imposing values and manipulating the news is increasingly difficult for governments and Great Powers.
uw: Treat a new information environment as a threat to be policed and you fall behind; treat it as terrain to be seized and you stay relevant — caution is a doctrine, not a strategy.
book: Seizing the Digital High Ground: Military Operations and Politics in the Social Media Era
author: author not named in IA metadata

title: Yemen: Comparative Insurgency and Counterinsurgency
steal: Yemen's counterinsurgency and counterterrorism policies were less effective against the Houthi movement than against AQAP because of four factors: the military's poor COIN/CT policies, the international effort's focus on AQAP, the Houthis' ability to recruit and mobilize large numbers of followers, and the Houthi leadership's pragmatic alliances — together these gave the Houthis the advantage over both AQAP and the Yemeni government.
why: Written in March 2015 as the Houthis captured Sanaa, it diagnosed the exact resilience mechanisms — mass mobilization plus pragmatic alliances — that explain how the Houthis survived a decade of war and now hold the Red Sea chokepoint.
uw: Counterinsurgency fails when it fights the wrong enemy first — the international fixation on AQAP left the Houthis room to out-organize and out-ally everyone.
author: Ryan Johnson

title: Complexity Theory and Its Applications in Linear Quantum Optics
steal: The 2010 discovery that the BosonSampling problem is likely hard for a classical computer to simulate opened a new technology path: passive linear optical networks with quantum states of light inherit the same computational hardness, and the intuitions behind BosonSampling led to developments in optical metrology suggesting quantum sensors could be viable within a few years with only marginal improvements in technology.
why: It traces how a result in abstract computational complexity becomes a sensor roadmap — the through-line from "a classical computer cannot efficiently simulate this" to deployable quantum metrology.
uw: Today's abstract complexity result is tomorrow's hardware — when a problem is provably hard classically, the physics that makes it hard is itself the technology.
book: Complexity Theory and Its Applications in Linear Quantum Optics
author: Jonathan P. Olson

title: Water Quality and Faecal Coliform Dynamics in Aquaculture Bheris of East Calcutta Wetland
steal: The East Kolkata Wetlands' "bheris" — shallow fish ponds fed by treated urban wastewater — are a century-old, Ramsar-recognized circular system that converts municipal sewage into protein; a six-month multi-site assessment found a notable improvement in the Water Quality Index across several sites and a significant reduction in faecal coliform counts, indicating growing suitability for sustainable aquaculture.
why: One of the world's oldest large-scale circular-economy food systems — a city farming fish in its own treated wastewater — and the measured trend is improving water quality, not declining.
uw: The most durable circular economies aren't new tech — Kolkata has been turning sewage into protein for a century; measure the system before assuming it's failing.
book: Water Quality and Faecal Coliform Dynamics in Aquaculture Bheris of East Calcutta Wetland
author: Rajashree Ghosh

title: The Housing Secure Initiative: Helping Families Overcome Housing Insecurity
steal: A church can attempt to move families from housing insecurity to housing security through deep, long-term relational community investment: RockPointe Church's Housing Secure Initiative was a 36-month journey with six Calgary families, treating them with the dignity and compassion the author sees modeled by Jesus, with the aim of transformation of people, families, communities, and nations.
why: It is a documented non-state, non-market intervention in the housing crisis — community-relationship capital as the mechanism, a small-sample practice-based counter-model to top-down housing policy.
uw: Housing insecurity is also a community deficit — long, committed relational support can attempt what neither the market nor the state delivers on its own.
book: The Housing Secure Initiative: Helping Families Overcome Housing Insecurity
author: Geoffrey Heth

title: Shinto is not ancestor-worship
steal: It is quite true that there is a large element of ancestor worship in modern Japanese religious practices, but a very little examination shows that all the great deities of the older Shinto are not Man, but Nature gods.
why: Corrects the most durable misunderstanding of Shinto — held even by most educated Japanese in Aston's day — by naming what the old gods actually were: Sun, Moon, Earth, Sea, Rain-storm, Fire, Thunder.
uw: When a belief about a tradition comes mostly from its modern packaging, check the founding layer — the ancestors may be younger than the gods.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: A religion of love, not fear
steal: It is rather, as Schiller called the worship of the gods of Greece, a Wonnedienst, a religion inspired by love and gratitude more than by fear.
why: Flips the default anthropology assumption — the saying 'Fear first made the Gods' does not hold here; the three greatest gods are beneficent beings and their festivals are occasions of rejoicing.
uw: When explaining why a religion endures, test the fear hypothesis against the love hypothesis — Shinto's staying power came from gratitude.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Kami are high, not infinite
steal: The Kami are high, swift, good, rich, living, but not infinite, omnipotent, or omniscient.
why: Defines the operating range of Shinto divinity: powerful superiors rather than an all-everything God — which is why they can be offended, propitiated, and kept at a ritual distance.
uw: When a system's gods have limits, read the religion as a technology for managing superiors rather than a metaphysics of the absolute.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Motoori's definition of Kami
steal: Not only human beings, but birds, beasts, plants and trees, seas and mountains, and all other things whatsoever which deserve to be dreaded and revered for the extraordinary and pre-eminent powers which they possess, are called Kami.
why: The widest working definition of divinity in the book — dread and reverence for extraordinary power, with no requirement of goodness, nobleness, or serviceableness.
uw: When deciding what counts as a 'god' in someone else's religion, use their criterion (dread-worthy power), not yours (moral perfection).
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Gods with no characters
steal: They are very feebly characterised. Indeed, most of them may be said to have no characters at all.
why: Aston's claim that the ancient Japanese imagination produced hundreds of deities but almost no personalities — polytheism without portraiture, distinct from the Greek model.
uw: When a pantheon feels thin, consider that weak characterization is the feature: gods as addressable powers, not characters.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Gods die of being forgotten
steal: There is a constant depletion in their ranks by the mere force of oblivion, while, on the other hand, new deities come into notice.
why: Worship as the life-support system of gods: without attention they sink into oblivion and new ones surface — divinity as an attention economy.
uw: When tracking which ideas survive in an organization, watch attention the way Shinto watches worship — what stops being noticed dies.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: The Sun-goddess is no autocrat
steal: Yet she is not what we should call a Supreme Deity. She is by no means an autocrat.
why: Even heaven's ruler — unrivalled in dignity, Ruler of Heaven — shares power with a Council of the Gods that decides important matters; Shinto's cosmos runs on distributed authority.
uw: When power looks absolute at the top, check for the council — Shinto's heaven is governed by committee, not decree.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: The mirror that is never opened
steal: It is kept in a bag of brocade which is never opened or repaired, a new one being added on the top of its predecessor when the latter is too much worn for further use.
why: Reverence maintained by refusing verification — the Sun-goddess's shintai at Ise is preserved by layering new wrappings over old, never looking inside.
uw: When a system's authority rests on something no one may inspect, expect the rule 'add a layer, never open' — that is how sacred objects stay sacred.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Priests with no cure of souls
steal: They have no 'cure of souls,' and their duties are confined to reading the litanies and seeing to the repairs of the shrine.
why: The Shinto priest as facilities manager, not shepherd — appointed by the civil authorities, indistinguishable from the laity off duty; religion as maintenance, not ministry.
uw: When a role looks priestly, check the job description — Shinto's kannushi maintains the building and reads the liturgy; souls are someone else's department.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Shrine means palace; festival means government
steal: Miya meant equally shrine and palace. Matsuri, a Shinto festival, is the same word that we also find in Matsurigoto, government.
why: The sacred and the secular were never separated in ancient Japan — the language itself fuses worship and rule, with the Mikado as high priest and sovereign at once.
uw: When analyzing a system where religion and state seem fused, look at the vocabulary — if one word does both jobs, the separation was never real.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Prayers are for material blessings only
steal: Shinto prayers are for material blessings only.
why: Rain in drought, good harvests, health, long life to the sovereign — the norito liturgies petition for outcomes in this world, never for salvation or the soul.
uw: When reading a prayer, note what it asks for — Shinto's ask list is entirely material, which tells you what the religion is for.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: The offence was ritual, the Jewish moral
steal: It is the crime of taking away human life which is condemned in the Decalogue: the Ohoharahi objects to wounds as nasty, unsightly things, unmeet for a God to look upon or to be in any way associated with. In a word, the Japanese offence was ritual, the Jewish moral.
why: The sharpest one-line comparative ethics in the book — self-inflicted wounds, the cutting of dead bodies, and justifiable homicide all polluted equally, because pollution is about unsightliness before the gods, not wrongness.
uw: When two rules look alike, compare the motive underneath — same prohibition, ritual motive versus moral motive, completely different religions.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: No ethics code as proof of goodness
steal: Shintoists do not deny this feature of their religion, but claim that the absence of a code of ethics is a proof of the superior natural goodness of the Japanese nation. It needs no such artificial aids to virtuous conduct.
why: The most audacious defense of a missing moral code in the book — the absence of ethics reframed as evidence of natural virtue rather than a gap.
uw: When someone defends the absence of a rule as proof of virtue, ask what happens when the virtue is tested — Aston spent the whole chapter showing the gap.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Buddhism swallowed the gods as avatars
steal: They discovered that whether Nature-gods or Man-gods they were nothing more than avatars or incarnations of the various Buddhas.
why: The mechanism of religious conquest by absorption — Buddhist missionaries did not refute Shinto's gods, they reclassified them as local forms of Buddhas, producing Ryobu Shinto.
uw: When a new system wants to win without a fight, watch for reclassification — the old gods survive by becoming avatars of the new ones.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: Shinto is doomed to extinction
steal: Without a code of morals, or an efficient ecclesiastical organisation, with little aid from the arts of painting, sculpture, and architecture, and with a sacred literature scanty and feeble compared with those of its foreign rivals, Shinto is doomed to extinction.
why: Aston's 1921 closing verdict — delivered with total confidence, and worth keeping as a card precisely because history gets to grade it: the religion he buried is still alive.
uw: When an expert declares a living tradition dead, keep the receipt — Aston wrote the obituary in 1921 and the patient survived him.
book: Shinto: The Ancient Religion of Japan
author: William George Aston

title: From successful defense to problematic offense: the devolution of unconventional warfare
steal: Unconventional warfare began in World War II as a defensive tactic for assisting an occupied ally, but Special Forces later redefined it to include offensive regime change; offensive UW, practiced extensively by the CIA during the Cold War, produced poor results, and it remains problematic — unreliable proxy forces, unpredictable outcomes, negative international perception. Defensive UW, under certain conditions, remains justified and practical.
why: It names the mechanism behind every proxy-war debate — backing someone else's fighters looks cheap until the proxies, the blowback, and the perception bill arrive. The CIA's own 2014 study (cited in the thesis) found arming rebels seldom works.
uw: Offense by proxy inherits everyone else's agency — if you can't vet the proxy, you can't own the outcome.
book: From successful defense to problematic offense: the devolution of unconventional warfare
author: Timothy S. Ball

title: Empirical analysis of using erasure coding in outsourcing data storage with provable security
steal: Proof of retrievability (POR) and proof of data possession (PDP) are cryptographic auditing tools that give probabilistic guarantees a server or cloud is actually storing your data — without downloading the whole file — and can recover the original data under certain limits; maximum distance separable (MDS) codes, specifically Reed-Solomon and Cauchy Reed-Solomon, are the recoverability engine, and the thesis surveys them and implements both into a prototype POR library built on the liberasurecode library.
why: Every "is my cloud copy intact?" guarantee rests on this primitive — verifying petabytes without re-downloading them is what makes outsourced storage auditable instead of faith-based.
uw: You don't need to hold the whole thing to prove it's intact — probabilistic proof beats full inspection; audit at the cheapest level that still binds.
book: Empirical analysis of using erasure coding in outsourcing data storage with provable security
author: Abdallah Bakir

title: A Validation of the Proposed Royal Australian Navy Standard Work Week and Naval Management Diary Using a Simulated Crew of an Armidale Class Patrol Boat
steal: Simulating a 21-member Armidale-class patrol boat crew in the Navy Management Diary over three weeks, the proposed RAN Navy Standard Work Week model breaks down in practice — the maintenance category most often exceeded its allocated hours, which the thesis says may warrant platform- and occupation-specific customization; and the NMD's fatigue tool versus the SAFTE model (FAST software) produced statistically significant differences in predicted risk, so the methodology should be replicated on a larger sample with real operational performance observations before comparing the two.
why: A work-week policy that looks fine on a spreadsheet and fails at the maintenance line is how a navy discovers fatigue in the field instead of on paper — the thesis is an argument that crew-endurance models must be validated against operations, not against each other.
uw: When two validated-looking models disagree significantly, the answer isn't to pick one — it's to test both against reality.
book: A Validation of the Proposed Royal Australian Navy Standard Work Week and Naval Management Diary Using a Simulated Crew of an Armidale Class Patrol Boat
author: Jessica Groot (Lieutenant

title: The West kept reforming instead of dying
steal: Western Civilization, on the contrary, did not pass from the Age of Crisis to the Age of Universal Empire, but instead was able to reform itself and entered upon a new period of expansion. Moreover, Western Civilization did this not once, but several times. It was this ability to reform or reorganize itself again and again which made Western Civilization the dominant factor in the world at the beginning of the twentieth century.
why: Quigley's whole theory pivots here: every other civilization went expansion, crisis, universal empire, decay — the West broke the cycle by reorganizing itself, repeatedly, instead of consolidating into one empire.
uw: When someone declares a civilization finished because its growth slowed — ask whether it is dying or reorganizing.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The four marks of an Age of Conflict
steal: (a) it is a period of declining rate of expansion; (b) it is a period of growing tensions and class conflicts; (c) it is a period of increasingly frequent and increasingly violent imperialist wars; and (d) it is a period of growing irrationality, pessimism, superstitions, and otherworldliness.
why: A diagnostic checklist for civilizational stall: the economics slow first, then the politics turn violent, then the culture turns superstitious — in that order, core before periphery.
uw: When growth stalls and the culture war gets weirder at the same time — check the sequence, not just the symptoms.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Expansion petrifies into vested interests
steal: In time, this system of commercial capitalism became petrified into a structure of vested interests in which profits were sought by imposing restrictions on the production or interchange of goods rather than by encouraging these activities.
why: The engine of every Quigley cycle: the organization that created the expansion hardens into the thing blocking the next one — profit shifts from making more to guarding what exists.
uw: When an industry's profits come from blocking entrants rather than serving customers — you are looking at petrification, not competition.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Four capitalists, four profit sources
steal: The commercial capitalist sought profits from the exchange of goods; the industrial capitalist sought profits from the manufacture of goods; the financial capitalist sought profits from the manipulation of claims on money; and the monopoly capitalist sought profits from manipulation of the market to make the market price and the amount sold such that his profits would be maximized.
why: Quigley's cleanest taxonomy: each stage of capitalism is defined by where profit is extracted — and each stage's profit source becomes the next stage's target for capture.
uw: When classifying a business or an era — ask where the profit actually comes from, not what the brochure says.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The financial capitalists at their worst
steal: The outbreak of war in 1914 showed these financial capitalists at their worst, narrow in outlook, ignorant, and selfish, while proclaiming, as usual, their total devotion to the social good.
why: Quigley, the insider-sympathizer, delivers his harshest verdict on the bankers at the exact moment their system met reality — expertise as performance, self-interest as public service.
uw: When the experts' models say a crisis is impossible and it happens anyway — remember who the models served.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Wars are not fought with gold
steal: Wars, as events have proved since, are not fought with gold or even with money, but by the proper organization of real resources.
why: The bankers' 1914 prediction — that the war must end in months for lack of gold — exposed the core fallacy: money is the scoreboard, organization is the game.
uw: When finance people explain why something cannot be done — check whether they are describing money or reality.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Four ways to pay for a war
steal: a. Taxation gives no inflation and no debt. b. Fiat money gives inflation and no debt. c. Bank credit gives inflation and debt. d. Sales of bonds give no inflation but give debt.
why: Sixteen words that decode a century of war finance: every government's funding mix is a choice about who pays — present taxpayers, savers, or the unborn.
uw: When a government announces how it will fund a crisis — run it through the four cells and see who is really paying.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: A world system of financial control in private hands
steal: the powers of financial capitalism had another far-reaching aim, nothing less than to create a world system of financial control in private hands able to dominate the political system of each country and the economy of the world as a whole. This system was to be controlled in a feudalist fashion by the central banks of the world acting in concert, by secret agreements arrived at in frequent private meetings and conferences.
why: Quigley's most-quoted claim, stated as the bankers' own program: not conspiracy theory but institutional design — private, feudal, coordinated through central banks, apexed at the BIS in Basle.
uw: When central bankers meet in Basle and markets move on the minutes — this is the architecture Quigley described.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: How central banks dominate governments
steal: Each central bank, in the hands of men like Montagu Norman of the Bank of England, Benjamin Strong of the New York Federal Reserve Bank, Charles Rist of the Bank of France, and Hjalmar Schacht of the Reichsbank, sought to dominate its government by its ability to control Treasury loans, to manipulate foreign exchanges, to influence the level of economic activity in the country, and to influence cooperative politicians by subsequent economic rewards in the business world.
why: The mechanism, named with names: dominance through Treasury loans, exchange manipulation, the business cycle itself — and the revolving door as the enforcement arm.
uw: When a central banker becomes a political oracle — ask which of the four levers is doing the talking.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The BIS: a private bank owned by central banks
steal: The B.I.S. as a private institution was owned by the seven chief central banks and was operated by the heads of these, who together formed its governing board. They made agreements on all the major financial problems of the world, as well as on many of the economic and political problems, especially in reference to loans, payments, and the economic future of the chief areas of the globe.
why: The apex of Quigley's system in one paragraph: a private bank, owned by central banks that were themselves private corporations, settling the world's money by bookkeeping instead of shipping gold.
uw: When someone says central banks are public institutions — the BIS charter says otherwise.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Rhodes's aim: federate the English-speaking peoples
steal: These purposes centered on his desire to federate the English-speaking peoples and to bring all the habitable portions of the world under their control. For this purpose Rhodes left part of his great fortune to found the Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford in order to spread the English ruling class tradition throughout the English-speaking world as Ruskin had wanted.
why: The motive behind the network, in Quigley's telling: the Rhodes Scholarships were not philanthropy but a personnel system — training an imperial ruling class under the cover of education.
uw: When an elite fellowship claims to be about merit — ask what ruling tradition it was built to spread.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The secret society of February 5, 1891
steal: This association was formally established on February 5, 1891, when Rhodes and Stead organized a secret society of which Rhodes had been dreaming for sixteen years. In this secret society Rhodes was to be leader; Stead, Brett (Lord Esher), and Milner were to form an executive committee; Arthur (Lord) Balfour, (Sir) Harry Johnston, Lord Rothschild, Albert (Lord) Grey, and others were listed as potential members of a "Circle of Initiates"; while there was to be an outer circle known as the "Association of Helpers" (later organized by Milner as the Round Table organization).
why: Quigley's documentary core for the network claim: a dated founding, a named executive committee, a Circle of Initiates, and an outer circle that became the Round Table — the organizational chart of the Anglo-American establishment.
uw: When tracing how an idea becomes policy across decades — look for the personnel network, not just the institutions.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: Five outlooks, from Enlightenment to Inclusive Diversity
steal: Over the past two centuries, there have been five such stages: the Enlightenment in 1730-1790, the Romantic Movement in 1790-1850, the Age of Scientific Materialism in 1850-1895, the Period of Irrational Activism of 1895-1945, and our new Age of Inclusive Diversity since 1945.
why: Quigley's cultural periodization: the twentieth century's new outlook is not a doctrine but a condition — diversity as the operating system, replacing the materialist certainties that ended in 1945.
uw: When a debate feels like two centuries talking past each other — check which outlook each side inhabits.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The twentieth century began in 1950
steal: The time covered by this book seems to this historian to fall into three periods: the nineteenth century from about 1814 to about 1895; the twentieth century, which did not begin until after World War II, perhaps as late as 1950; and a long period of transition from 1895 to 1950.
why: Quigley's dating refuses the calendar: the 'twentieth century' is not 1900-1999 but the postwar order — and 1895-1950 was a 55-year transition, one of the most awful periods in all human history.
uw: When periodizing any era — date it by the system change, not the round number.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: War and depression are man-made, and needless
steal: The hope of the twentieth century rests on its recognition that war and depression are man-made, and needless.
why: The entire 1,300-page tragedy compressed into the hope: if the catastrophes were made by human choices, they can be unmade by human choices — the book's title in one sentence.
uw: When catastrophe is framed as inevitable — ask who made it, and who benefits from the framing.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The nineteenth century's epitaph
steal: the nineteenth century was, however hopeful in its general processes, a period of materialism, selfishness, false values, hypocrisy, and secret vices.
why: Quigley refuses nostalgia for the pre-1914 world: the horrors of 1914-1945 did not come from nowhere — they were the nineteenth century's underlying evils emerging 'in all their nakedness.'
uw: When someone romanticizes a golden age — ask what evils were working underneath it.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The international Anglophile network
steal: There does exist, and has existed for a generation, an international Anglophile network which operates, to some extent, in the way the ... Right believes the Communists act. In fact, this network, which we may identify as the Round Table Groups, has no aversion to cooperating with the Communists, or any other groups, and frequently does so. I know of the operations of this network because I have studied it for twenty years and was permitted for two years, in the early 1960's, to examine its papers and secret records.
why: The book's most famous admission, in Quigley's own voice: a named network — the Round Table Groups — operating internationally for a generation, studied by him for twenty years with two years of access to its papers and secret records.
uw: When the establishment is dismissed as a figure of speech — Quigley studied this one for twenty years and read its secret records.
author: Carroll Quigley

title: The naturalness of acquiring
steal: The wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame.
why: Sets the book’s moral frame: expansion itself is natural and praiseworthy; only incompetent expansion is folly.
uw: When someone moralizes ambition itself instead of how it is pursued.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: The innovator’s enemies
steal: And it ought to be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new.
why: The original statement of why reform is hard: the old order’s beneficiaries fight, the new order’s beneficiaries don’t believe yet.
uw: When a reform or reorg stalls and you need the mechanism, not the morale speech.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: Severities, properly used
steal: Those may be called properly used, if of evil it is possible to speak well, that are applied at one blow and are necessary to one’s security, and that are not persisted in afterwards unless they can be turned to the advantage of the subjects.
why: The economy of cruelty: all necessary harm at one stroke, then benefits; the drip-feed of harm is what loses states.
uw: When debating whether to rip the bandage off.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: The real truth of the matter
steal: But, it being my intention to write a thing which shall be useful to him who apprehends it, it appears to me more appropriate to follow up the real truth of the matter than the imagination of it; for many have pictured republics and principalities which in fact have never been known or seen, because how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, that he who neglects what is done for what ought to be done, sooner effects his ruin than his preservation
why: The book’s method in one line: study what is done, not what ought to be done, because the distance between them ruins the virtuous.
uw: When a plan is built on how people should behave.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: Feared, not loved
steal: It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with. Because this is to be asserted in general of men, that they are ungrateful, fickle, false, cowardly, covetous, and as long as you succeed they are yours entirely; they will offer you their blood, property, life, and children, as is said above, when the need is far distant; but when it approaches they turn against you.
why: Love is voluntary and fickle; fear is a bond you control. The cold logic of relying on other men’s promises.
uw: When trust is being treated as a strategy.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: The fox and the lion
steal: so it is necessary for a prince to know how to make use of both natures, and that one without the other is not durable. A prince, therefore, being compelled knowingly to adopt the beast, ought to choose the fox and the lion; because the lion cannot defend himself against snares and the fox cannot defend himself against wolves. Therefore, it is necessary to be a fox to discover the snares and a lion to terrify the wolves.
why: Force without cunning walks into snares; cunning without force cannot hold what it takes. One without the other is not durable.
uw: When someone is all-lawyer or all-muscle.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: Judge by the result
steal: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them; and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.
why: The many see the surface and the few who see through it dare not contradict the many — outcomes launder methods.
uw: When a winner’s methods go unexamined.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: Fortune favors the bold
steal: For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly.
why: Fortune is changeful and men are steadfast in their ways; boldness is the only stance that can master chance.
uw: When caution is being sold as prudence in a volatile moment.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli

title: The morning briefing
steal: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man.
why: Pre-decide your response to difficult people before the day starts — the obstacle named in advance loses its ambush.
uw: When you walk into a day of difficult people.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: The inner citadel
steal: At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses. A man cannot any whither retire better than to his own soul; he especially who is beforehand provided of such things within, which whensoever he doth withdraw himself to look in, may presently afford unto him perfect ease and tranquillity.
why: The one retreat no circumstance can take: tranquillity as an inward order, not a place.
uw: When escape feels like the only option.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: Get up — it is your work
steal: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
why: Duty reframed as nature: you were made for the work, not the warm bed.
uw: When the snooze button is winning the argument.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: The soul takes the dye of its thoughts
steal: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time. For the soul doth as it were receive its tincture from the fancies, and imaginations. Dye it therefore and thoroughly soak it with the assiduity of these cogitations.
why: Attention is the mechanism of character: soak the mind deliberately, or it soaks up whatever surrounds it.
uw: When choosing what to feed your attention.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: The best revenge
steal: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
why: Retaliation is assimilation — the only clean victory is refusing the opponent’s shape.
uw: When revenge feels righteous.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: See things unadorned
steal: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with the blood of a shellfish.
why: The Stoic stripping exercise: name things by what they physically are and the added glamour falls off.
uw: When luxury or status is doing your thinking for you.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: Use the impediment
steal: So may every reasonable creature, what crosses and impediments soever it meets with in the course of this mortal life, it may use them as fit and proper objects, to the furtherance of whatsoever it intended and absolutely proposed unto itself as its natural end and happiness.
why: The obstacle as raw material: whatever blocks the action can be made the object of the action.
uw: When a setback looks like the end of the plan.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: Nobody can hinder the right act
steal: there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.
why: The inner-freedom claim: no one can stop you from doing and speaking what accords with your nature.
uw: When external pressure is the excuse.
author: Marcus Aurelius

title: Equality, the providential fact
steal: The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it possesses all the characteristics of a divine decree: it is universal, it is durable, it constantly eludes all human interference, and all events as well as all men contribute to its progress.
why: The book’s generative claim: equality of conditions is a divine-decree-level force no generation can check.
uw: When democratic trends are treated as reversible policy choices.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: The fundamental fact
steal: The more I advanced in the study of American society, the more I perceived that the equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.
why: Tocqueville’s method in one line: find the single fact from which all others derive.
uw: When drowning in symptoms and you need the root.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: Association, the mother science
steal: In democratic countries the science of association is the mother of science; the progress of all the rest depends upon the progress it has made.
why: In democracies the art of associating is the master skill on which civilization depends.
uw: When collective action fails and the proposed fix is a hero.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: Individualism, defined
steal: Individualism is a mature and calm feeling, which disposes each member of the community to sever himself from the mass of his fellow-creatures; and to draw apart with his family and his friends; so that, after he has thus formed a little circle of his own, he willingly leaves society at large to itself.
why: The distinction that runs the book: individualism is a calm error of judgment, egotism a blind passion. Tocqueville coined the word for the new disease.
uw: When withdrawal gets mislabeled as selfishness.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: Association against the majority
steal: At the present time the liberty of association is become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority.
why: The institutional answer to majority tyranny: not rights on paper but the organized habit of combining.
uw: When a majority starts closing ranks.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: Soft despotism
steal: Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. That power is absolute, minute, regular, provident, and mild. It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood
why: The famous prophecy: a mild, absolute, minute power that keeps men in perpetual childhood and spares them the trouble of living.
uw: When comfort is being traded for agency.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: The apprenticeship of liberty
steal: It cannot be repeated too often that nothing is more fertile in prodigies than the art of being free; but there is nothing more arduous than the apprenticeship of liberty.
why: Freedom is fertile but its apprenticeship is arduous — despotism’s temporary prosperity is the trap.
uw: When liberty looks like too much trouble.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: The sad Americans
steal: In America I saw the freest and most enlightened men, placed in the happiest circumstances which the world affords: it seemed to me as if a cloud habitually hung upon their brow, and I thought them serious and almost sad even in their pleasures.
why: The paradox of prosperity: the freest men brooding over advantages they do not possess, feverishly pursuing welfare.
uw: When success does not feel like it.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: The press, last bulwark
steal: but that servitude cannot be complete if the press is free: the press is the chiefest democratic instrument of freedom.
why: Parliaments and popular sovereignty can coexist with servitude; a free press cannot.
uw: When press freedom is treated as one liberty among many.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

title: The invisible government
steal: The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society. Those who manipulate this unseen mechanism of society constitute an invisible government which is the true ruling power of our country. We are governed, our minds are molded, our tastes formed, our ideas suggested, largely by men we have never heard of.
why: The book’s opening thesis: democracy is governed by unseen manipulators of mass habit — a structural feature, not a conspiracy.
uw: When “who really decides?” is the question.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: The executive arm
steal: Propaganda is the executive arm of the invisible government.
why: Propaganda named as the operating machinery of the invisible government — every social project runs on it.
uw: When someone thinks propaganda is only a wartime word.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: Rubber-stamp minds
steal: But instead of a mind, universal literacy has given him rubber stamps, rubber stamps inked with advertising slogans, with editorials, with published scientific data, with the trivialities of the tabloids and the platitudes of history, but quite innocent of original thought. Each man’s rubber stamps are the duplicates of millions of others, so that when those millions are exposed to the same stimuli, all receive identical imprints.
why: Literacy did not produce independent minds; it produced identical imprints from identical stimuli — the precondition of mass persuasion.
uw: When everyone suddenly agrees.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: The intelligent minorities
steal: clearly it is the intelligent minorities which need to make use of propaganda continuously and systematically. In the active proselytizing minorities in whom selfish interests and public interests coincide lie the progress and development of America. Only through the active energy of the intelligent few can the public at large become aware of and act upon new ideas. Small groups of persons can, and do, make the rest of us think what they please about a given subject.
why: Bernays’s open claim: progress comes from small groups making the rest think what they please; minorities use propaganda continuously.
uw: When a fringe idea goes mainstream overnight.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: Reach the group leaders
steal: To reach and persuade the group leaders who dictate the public’s thoughts and actions is likewise expensive. For this reason there is an increasing tendency to concentrate the functions of propaganda in the hands of the propaganda specialist.
why: The targeting doctrine: persuade the leaders who dictate the public’s thoughts and the group follows — hence the propaganda specialist.
uw: When planning how an idea actually spreads.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: The PR counsel, defined
steal: The public relations counsel, then, is the agent who, working with modern media of communication and the group formations of society, brings an idea to the consciousness of the public.
why: The job description of the new profession: bringing ideas to public consciousness via media and group formations.
uw: When “PR” needs distinguishing from advertising.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: Induce our leaders to lead
steal: The great political problem in our modern democracy is how to induce our leaders to lead. The dogma that the voice of the people is the voice of God tends to make elected persons the will-less servants of their constituents.
why: The democratic paradox: the voice-of-God dogma makes elected men will-less servants, producing political sterility.
uw: When leaders only follow polls.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: Influence the leaders, sway the herd
steal: If you can influence the leaders, either with or without their conscious coöperation, you automatically influence the group which they sway.
why: Mass psychology works without the mass: man feels himself a herd member alone in his room, so moving the leader moves the group.
uw: When a message needs scale without a crowd.
author: Edward L. Bernays

title: The five filters
steal: The essential ingredients of our propaganda model, or set of news “filters,” fall under the following headings: (1) the size, concentrated ownership, owner wealth, and profit orientation of the dominant mass-media firms; (2) advertising as the primary income source of the mass media; (3) the reliance of the media on information provided by government, business, and “experts” funded and approved by these primary sources and agents of power; (4) “flak” as a means of disciplining the media; and (5) “anticommunism” as a national religion and control mechanism. The raw material of news must pass through successive filters, leaving only the cleansed residue fit to print.
why: The entire model in one paragraph: five structural filters decide what counts as news before any reporter writes a word.
uw: When someone asks how propaganda works in a country with no censorship.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Objectivity inside the filters
steal: The elite domination of the media and marginalization of dissidents that results from the operation of these filters occurs so naturally that media news people, frequently operating with complete integrity and goodwill, are able to convince themselves that they choose and interpret the news “objectively” and on the basis of professional news values.
why: No conspiracy is required: sincere journalists can report objectively within limits they never chose.
uw: When “but reporters mean well” is used to dismiss media critique.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: A Private Ministry of Information
steal: Ben Bagdikian stresses the fact that despite the large media numbers, the twenty-nine largest media systems account for over half of the output of newspapers, and most of the sales and audiences in magazines, broadcasting, books, and movies. He contends that these “constitute a new Private Ministry of Information and Culture” that can set the national agenda.
why: Twenty-five thousand media entities, twenty-nine setting the agenda — ownership concentration as the first filter, with 1986 numbers.
uw: When the sheer number of outlets is offered as proof of press freedom.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: A voting system weighted by income
steal: In short, the mass media are interested in attracting audiences with buying power, not audiences per se; it is affluent audiences that spark advertiser interest today, as in the nineteenth century. The idea that the drive for large audiences makes the mass media “democratic” thus suffers from the initial weakness that its political analogue is a voting system weighted by income!
why: The advertising filter's core logic: the audience is the product, and only affluent buyers count.
uw: When reach and ratings get mistaken for democratic representation.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Excessive objectivity
steal: Barnouw notes that although at that time a great many large companies were spending money on commercials and other publicity regarding environmental problems, the documentary series failed for want of sponsors. The problem was one of excessive objectivity in the series, which included suggestions of corporate or systemic failure, whereas the corporate message “was one of reassurance.”
why: An NBC environmental series died not for bias but for objectivity — sponsors wanted reassurance, not systemic failure.
uw: When someone asks how advertisers shape content without issuing orders.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: The symbiotic relationship
steal: The mass media are drawn into a symbiotic relationship with powerful sources of information by economic necessity and reciprocity of interest. The media need a steady, reliable flow of the raw material of news. They have daily news demands and imperative news schedules that they must meet.
why: The sourcing filter: beats, press conferences, and official leaks are cheaper than reporting — so power becomes the default source.
uw: When official sources dominate a story and nobody asks why.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Bureaucratic affinity
steal: Mark Fishman calls this “the principle of bureaucratic affinity: only other bureaucracies can satisfy the input needs of a news bureaucracy.”
why: Why the White House, the Pentagon, and city hall are the permanent news beats: newsrooms are bureaucracies that can only feed on other bureaucracies.
uw: When mapping why some voices are always quoted and others never are.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Flak as discipline
steal: “Flak” refers to negative responses to a media statement or program. It may take the form of letters, telegrams, phone calls, petitions, lawsuits, speeches and bills before Congress, and other modes of complaint, threat, and punitive action. If certain kinds of fact, position, or program are thought likely to elicit flak, this prospect can be a deterrent.
why: The fourth filter: punishment doesn't have to arrive — the anticipation of it is enough to kill a story.
uw: When a story dies quietly and nobody gave an order.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: The fuzzy enemy
steal: This ideology helps mobilize the populace against an enemy, and because the concept is fuzzy it can be used against anybody advocating policies that threaten property interests or support accommodation with Communist states and radicalism.
why: The fifth filter's genius: a fuzzy enemy label that can be aimed at anyone who threatens property interests.
uw: When a vague ideological label gets deployed against a domestic policy.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: The commissar instruction
steal: The mass media never explain why Andrei Sakharov is worthy and José Luis Massera, in Uruguay, is unworthy—the attention and general dichotomization occur “naturally” as a result of the working of the filters, but the result is the same as if a commissar had instructed the media: “Concentrate on the victims of enemy powers and forget about the victims of friends.”
why: The book's most quoted line: dichotomization happens naturally, but lands exactly where a censor's order would.
uw: When coverage of foreign victims tracks official enemies and friends.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Worthy and unworthy victims
steal: A propaganda system will consistently portray people abused in enemy states as worthy victims, whereas those treated with equal or greater severity by its own government or clients will be unworthy.
why: The paired-comparison method of the whole book: worth is assigned by politics, read off the volume and tone of coverage.
uw: When comparing how two similar atrocities get covered.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Pol Pot's changing worth
steal: The victims of Pol Pot, a Communist leader, were worthy, although after he was ousted by the Vietnamese in 1978, Cambodians ceased to be worthy, as U.S. policy shifted toward support of Pol Pot in exile.
why: The same dead, worthy then unworthy: victimhood tracks U.S. policy shifts, not the scale of suffering.
uw: When a victim group suddenly drops out of the news.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Demonstration elections
steal: The United States organized what have been called “demonstration elections” in its client states, defined as those whose primary function is to convince the home population that the intervention is well intentioned, that the populace of the invaded and occupied country welcomes the intrusion, and that they are being given a democratic choice.
why: Elections as stagecraft for the home audience: El Salvador's vote legitimized, Nicaragua's delegitimized, by the same press.
uw: When a foreign election is sold as proof of democracy.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: No conspiracy required
steal: We do not use any kind of “conspiracy” hypothesis to explain massmedia performance. In fact, our treatment is much closer to a “free market” analysis, with the results largely an outcome of the workings of market forces. Most biased choices in the media arise from the preselection of right-thinking people, internalized preconceptions, and the adaptation of personnel to the constraints of ownership, organization, market, and political power. Censorship is largely self-censorship, by reporters and commentators who adjust to the realities of source and media organizational requirements.
why: The authors' preemptive defense: this is market analysis, not conspiracy — bias comes from hiring, habit, and self-censorship.
uw: When the model gets dismissed as a conspiracy theory.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Fixing the premises of discourse
steal: The special importance of propaganda in what Walter Lippmann referred to as the “manufacture of consent” has long been recognized by writers on public opinion, propaganda, and the political requirements of social order. The powerful are able to fix the premises of discourse, to decide what the general populace is allowed to see, hear, and think about, and to “manage” public opinion by regular propaganda campaigns.
why: The title's thesis: power doesn't need to win arguments — it sets what arguments are allowed to happen.
uw: When the debate feels lively but the boundaries feel fixed.
author: Noam Chomsky & Edward S. Herman

title: Power is what the enemy thinks you have
steal: Always remember the first rule of power tactics: Power is not only what you have but what the enemy thinks you have.
why: Power is perception: the size of your force is measured in the enemy's head, not in your headcount.
uw: When you're outnumbered and need to look bigger than you are.
author: Saul D. Alinsky

title: Never go outside the experience of your people
steal: The second rule is: Never go outside the experience of your people. When an action or tactic is outside the experience of the people, the result is confusion, fear, and retreat. It also means a collapse of communication, as we have noted.
why: Novelty in tactics backfires on your own side first — your people retreat before the enemy even reacts.
uw: Before trying a tactic your people have never seen before.
author: Saul D. Alinsky

title: Go outside the experience of the enemy
steal: The third rule is: Wherever possible go outside of the experience of the enemy. Here you want to cause confusion, fear, and retreat.
why: The mirror of rule two: unfamiliar tactics are a weapon only when pointed at the other side.
uw: When you're planning how the enemy will react to something new.
author: Saul D. Alinsky

title: Make the enemy live up to its own book of rules
steal: The fourth rule is: Make the enemy live up to their own book of rules. You can kill them with this, for they can no more obey their own rules than the Christian church can live up to Christianity.
why: No institution can survive full compliance with its own stated standards — so demand exactly that.
uw: When an institution preaches one thing and practices another.
author: Saul D. Alinsky

title: Ridicule is man's most potent weapon
steal: The fourth rule carries within it the fifth rule: Ridicule is man's most potent weapon. It is almost impossible to counterattack ridicule. Also it infuriates the opposition, who then react to your advantage.
why: Laughter can't be answered with a press release — and an angry opponent makes your mistakes for you.
uw: When the other side's dignity is its armor.
author: Saul D. Alinsky

title: A good tactic is one your people enjoy
