"to show that I was not above my business, I sometimes brought home the paper I purchas'd at the stores thro' the streets on a wheelbarrow."
why: A new printer with debts needed credit. He managed the visible signs of industry as carefully as the work itself. By his account the stationery merchants then "solicited my custom."
uw: Your work is solid but the people who decide on credit or business never see it.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: A club where every member owes a question
steal:
"every member, in his turn, should produce one or more queries on any point of Morals, Politics, or Natural Philosophy, to be discuss'd by the company; and once in three months produce and read an essay of his own writing"

"all expressions of positiveness in opinions, or direct contradiction, were after some time made contraband, and prohibited under small pecuniary penalties."
why: The Junto required output from everyone: a query each turn, an essay each quarter, queries read a week ahead. Heat was priced with small fines. The library, the fire company and the branch clubs all came out of it.
uw: Your discussion group talks a lot, produces nothing, and keeps sliding into debate.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Call it a scheme of a number of friends
steal: "I therefore put myself as much as I could out of sight, and stated it as a scheme of a number of friends, who had requested me to go about and propose it to such as they thought lovers of reading. In this way my affair went on more smoothly, and I ever after practis'd it on such occasions"
why: Asking neighbors to fund his library raised the suspicion that he wanted to rise above them. Hiding his authorship removed the objection. He used the same cover for the academy pamphlet, published as the work of "publick-spirited gentlemen."
uw: Your project needs other people's money or help and your name on it is causing resistance.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: A black spot for every fault
steal: "I rul'd each page with red ink, so as to have seven columns, one for each day of the week, marking each column with a letter for the day. I cross'd these columns with thirteen red lines, marking the beginning of each line with the first letter of one of the virtues, on which line, and in its proper column, I might mark, by a little black spot, every fault I found upon examination to have been committed respecting that virtue upon that day."
why: The book reproduces the thirteen precepts and a sample page. He defined each virtue narrowly enough to check daily, and the page kept the count instead of his memory. "I was surpris'd to find myself so much fuller of faults than I had imagined" is his report of the results.
uw: You keep resolving to change a habit and have no record of how often you slip.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Weed one bed at a time
steal: "like him who, having a garden to weed, does not attempt to eradicate all the bad herbs at once, which would exceed his reach and his strength, but works on one of the beds at a time"
why: He gave each virtue a week of strict attention and kept the earlier lines clear while adding the next. Thirteen virtues made "a course compleat in thirteen weeks, and four courses in a year."
uw: You are trying to fix everything at once and none of it is sticking.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: 'I think I like a speckled ax best'
steal: "'No,' said the smith, 'turn on, turn on; we shall have it bright by-and-by; as yet, it is only speckled.' 'Yes,' says the man, 'but I think I like a speckled ax best.'"
why: Order was the virtue he could not master. He tells the ax story against himself: the man tired of turning the wheel and called the half-done job his preference. Franklin says something "that pretended to be reason" made him the same offer.
uw: You are about to lower a standard and call it a preference.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Put the proverbs in the almanac's empty spaces
steal:
"I consider'd it as a proper vehicle for conveying instruction among the common people, who bought scarcely any other books; I therefore filled all the little spaces that occurr'd between the remarkable days in the calendar with proverbial sentences"

"The bringing all these scatter'd councils thus into a focus enabled them to make greater impression."
why: He put his message in the one book people already bought, then gathered the proverbs into a single speech, The Way to Wealth (in the Appendix). The sales and reprint figures are his.
uw: Your message has no audience of its own and there is a channel people already read.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Borrow the rival's scarce book
steal:
"Having heard that he had in his library a certain very scarce and curious book, I wrote a note to him, expressing my desire of perusing that book, and requesting he would do me the favour of lending it to me for a few days."

"He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged."
why: A new Assembly member had spoken against him. Franklin asked a small favor instead of offering one, returned the book in a week with thanks, and says they "became great friends." The outcome is his account.
uw: Someone with influence over you dislikes you and doing them favors hasn't helped.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Fifty subscribers at forty shillings
steal:
"by thus clubbing our books to a common library, we should, while we lik'd to keep them together, have each of us the advantage of using the books of all the other members"

"fifty persons, mostly young tradesmen, willing to pay down for this purpose forty shillings each, and ten shillings per annum."
why: The Junto first pooled its own books in one room. When that worked, he turned it into a subscription: small payments from many people, renewed each year. He calls it "the mother of all the North American subscription libraries"; that is his claim.
uw: You need to fund something useful and no single patron will pay for it.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Render accounts with great clearness
steal: "they should always render accounts, and make remittances, with great clearness and punctuality."
why: His Charleston partner, honest but "ignorant in matters of account," never sent a clear statement. The partner's widow, schooled in accounts in Holland, reported every quarter and kept the business paying. Bradford lost the postmaster's commission over inexact accounts, and Franklin got it.
uw: You handle other people's money or affairs and want more of their trust.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: The winner at chess sets the grammar
steal: "I at length refus'd to play any more, unless on this condition, that the victor in every game should have a right to impose a task, either in parts of the grammar to be got by heart, or in translations, etc., which tasks the vanquish'd was to perform upon honour, before our next meeting. As we play'd pretty equally, we thus beat one another into that language."
why: Chess was eating the time he and a friend had set aside for Italian. He kept the game and made the loser pay in study.
uw: A habit you enjoy is eating the time meant for something you need to learn.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: The regret is the same either way
steal:
"In 1736 I lost one of my sons, a fine boy of four years old, by the small-pox, taken in the common way. I long regretted bitterly, and still regret that I had not given it to him by inoculation."

"my example showing that the regret may be the same either way, and that, therefore, the safer should be chosen."
why: Parents skipped inoculation because they feared regretting a death they had caused. He lost his son to the disease and regretted it all the same. When both choices carry regret, the regret cannot decide; the odds should.
uw: You are avoiding the safer choice because you fear regretting it if it goes wrong.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Branch clubs that don't know they are branches
steal:
"every member separately should endeavour to form a subordinate club, with the same rules respecting queries, etc., and without informing them of the connection with the Junto."

"the Junto member might propose what queries we should desire, and was to report to the Junto what pass'd in his separate club"
why: Each Junto member started a club on the same rules. The branches fed back the town's opinion and spread proposals "as arising in each of them." Five or six were formed. Their effect on later measures is his account.
uw: You need to know what a wider group thinks and to put ideas in front of it without a central sponsor.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Fines for missed meetings buy the fire engines
steal:
"Our articles of agreement oblig'd every member to keep always in good order, and fit for use, a certain number of leather buckets, with strong bags and baskets (for packing and transporting of goods), which were to be brought to every fire"

"The small fines that have been paid by members for absence at the monthly meetings have been apply'd to the purchase of fire-engines, ladders, fire-hooks, and other useful implements for each company"
why: The Union Fire Company wrote each member's duty into the articles and turned absence into equipment. The city's fire record he gives afterward is his claim.
uw: You are starting a volunteer group and need both attendance and gear without a budget.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Make the grant conditional so the clause works both ways
steal:
"it shall and may be lawful for the said speaker, and he is hereby required, to sign an order on the provincial treasurer for the payment of two thousand pounds"

"we urg'd the conditional promise of the law as an additional motive to give, since every man's donation would be doubled; thus the clause work'd both ways."
why: The Assembly doubted the hospital could raise two thousand pounds privately. Franklin wrote the grant to pay only when it did, which cost the doubters nothing to pass. Donors then heard their money would be doubled. The clause is reproduced in the book; the outcome is his account.
uw: The funder doubts you can raise the rest, and the donors want to know their money counts.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Write the wagon terms from the owners' side
steal:
"three or four of such as cannot separately spare from the business of their plantations a waggon and four horses and a driver, may do it together, one furnishing the waggon, another one or two horses, and another the driver, and divide the pay proportionately between you"

"The owners, however, alleging they did not know General Braddock, or what dependence might be had on his promise, insisted on my bond for the performance, which I accordingly gave them."
why: Braddock had found twenty-five wagons. Franklin's printed advertisement set pay in advance, appraisal of horses, shared teams, and the threat of soldiers seizing them otherwise. The advertisement is reproduced; the 150 wagons and his near-ruin over the claims are his account.
uw: You are asked to get something from people who have no reason to trust the person asking.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Let the papers shift for themselves
steal: "I concluded to let my papers shift for themselves, believing it was better to spend what time I could spare from public business in making new experiments, than in disputing about those already made."
why: The Abbé Nollet attacked his electrical work in print. His experiments could be repeated by anyone, so an answer would add nothing. He kept working. That Nollet lived "to see himself the last of his sect" is his account.
uw: A critic attacks work that others can check, and a reply would cost time you need for the next piece.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: A friend's list of instances adds Humility
steal: "a Quaker friend having kindly informed me that I was generally thought proud; that my pride show'd itself frequently in conversation; that I was not content with being in the right when discussing any point, but was overbearing, and rather insolent, of which he convinc'd me by mentioning several instances"
why: His list had twelve virtues. The friend's examples, not a principle, added the thirteenth. Franklin admits he got the appearance of humility more than the reality.
uw: Someone you trust names a fault of yours and backs it with specific instances.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Proud of my humility
steal: "Disguise it, struggle with it, beat it down, stifle it, mortify it as much as one pleases, it is still alive, and will every now and then peep out and show itself; you will see it, perhaps, often in this history; for, even if I could conceive that I had compleatly overcome it, I should probably be proud of my humility."
why: Claiming victory over pride is itself pride. He tells the reader to look for it in this memoir.
uw: You are about to announce that you have beaten a flaw.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Don't give too much for the whistle
steal: "This, however, was afterwards of use to me, the impression continuing on my mind; so that often, when I was tempted to buy some unnecessary thing, I said to myself, Don't give too much for the whistle; and I saved my money."
why: At seven he gave all his coppers for a whistle and his family told him he had paid four times its worth. He kept the phrase as a price check, then applied it to courtiers, misers and men who chase popularity.
uw: You are about to pay for something you wanted on sight.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Emptying your pockets at home won't save you
steal: "As he proceeded I began to soften, and concluded to give the coppers. Another stroke of his oratory made me asham'd of that, and determin'd me to give the silver; and he finish'd so admirably, that I empty'd my pocket wholly into the collector's dish, gold and all."
why: He had "silently resolved" Whitefield would get nothing. A friend at the same sermon had emptied his pockets before leaving home and still tried to borrow money to give. Neither man's advance decision survived the sermon.
uw: You are walking into a strong pitch you have already decided to refuse.
author: Benjamin Franklin

title: Write the means and manner, skip the exhortation
steal: "I should have called my book The Art of Virtue, because it would have shown the means and manner of obtaining virtue, which would have distinguished it from the mere exhortation to be good, that does not instruct and indicate the means"
why: He planned a book that taught method rather than urging goodness, and compared exhortation to telling the hungry to be fed. He never wrote it. The memoir's chapter on the virtue table is the closest he came.
uw: You are about to tell someone what to be without telling them how.
